body.text: In short:
Christa Pike awoke "angry and confused" in a hospital this week, with her first words being: "Where am I?"
The 50-year-old convicted killer survived a botched execution after receiving two lethal doses of pentobarbital a week ago.
What's next?
A US judge has ordered the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve all evidence related to the botched execution of Christa Pike.
Convicted killer Christa Pike has woken up "angry and confused", with her first words being "where am I?" her attorney says.

The 50-year-old was rushed to hospital last week following two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital, inside the death chamber at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, Tennessee.
She had been sentenced to death for the torture and murder of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in 1996, a crime committed when she was 18 years old.
Pike regained consciousness yesterday and was aware of her botched execution, her lawyers said.
"On Monday night, it was our understanding that Christa was brain dead and that life support would be removed the next day," Mr Spivey said.
"But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone … Christa woke up and began talking."
Mr Spivey, who was not with Pike when she woke up, said he was told her first words were: "Where am I?" and "Who are you?"
Her lawyers said she still could not move her arms or swallow, her prognosis remained unclear and that she had a long road to recovery.
Christa Pike's attorneys want evidence preserved
The failed execution has renewed scrutiny of how states carry out the death penalty, in particular the use of lethal injection.
A judge in the US state of Tennessee ordered authorities to preserve evidence related to the execution.
Pike's lawyers filed an emergency court motion.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, she is the first person to survive the administration of lethal injection drugs in the US.
He attorney, Luke Ihnen, told the court on Wednesday, local time, Pike was "speaking limitedly".
At the hearing in Nashville, Mr Ihnen asked the court to order the Tennessee Department of Correction to save evidence in the case and provide more information about what went wrong.
The judge ordered the state to preserve "anything that was in the actual room".

"Part of the issue that we are facing is up until yesterday, our client was unconscious, unable to communicate with counsel, unable to communicate with medical providers, and without her consent" a new lawsuit cannot be filed, Mr Ihnen told the court.
Her legal team said that Pike's prognosis remained unclear and, at a minimum, she faced a lengthy recovery.
Her arms were burned and blistered after the attempted lethal injection and she was handcuffed to a hospital bed, they said.
Pike's attorneys wanted the court order to require the prison system to preserve information from the attempted execution, including drug lot numbers, needles, execution logs and other information.

Chancery Court Judge I'Ashea Myles indicated that her order to save the evidence would be sweeping, saying the state should maintain recordings, witness accounts and emails along with drugs, syringes, IV lines and other medical items.
The Tennessee Attorney General's Office said a court order was unnecessary. Assistant Attorney General John W Ayers said evidence from the death chamber had already been collected and logged.

Governor Bill Lee, a Republican, has called what happened "deeply disturbing" and ordered a "comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred". The governor postponed the state's only other execution scheduled for this year.
Tennessee's prison chief resigned in the wake of the failed execution, which has renewed scrutiny of how states carry out the death penalty, in particular the use of lethal injection.
Christa Pike's recovery remains uncertain
Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on the possibility that a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in Pike's tissue rather than entering her bloodstream.
Pike's lawyers wrote in their court filing that "apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realise that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown".
The attempted execution got underway around 7:30pm on September 30, when Pike was given a chance to make a final statement.
About five minutes later, Pike raised her head and said her arm was hurting.
At some point she appeared to lose consciousness, but she could be heard audibly breathing until media were escorted from the witness room at 8:53pm.
An ambulance arrived at the prison at 9:14pm to take Pike to a hospital.

Joel Zivot, a professor of anaesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike's legal team, said it could be weeks or months before anyone knew exactly what her recovery might look like, and whether her competency could be restored so the state could try again to execute her.
Wires/ABC
